newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S.'s Albright prepares to visit a troubled Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: U.S.'s Albright prepares to visit a troubled Bosnia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright travels to Bosnia this weekend amid growing international concern that a peace treaty which ended a bitter war in the country late in 1995 may be unravelling.
Nationalist parties that helped ignite the conflict are more powerful than ever, ignoring any provision of the peace agreement which they deem to be inconvenient.
Refugees who try to cross former front lines to return to their homes are stoned or beaten and some are killed.
Much of the reconstruction aid offered by international donors has yet to be dispersed because of interminable quarrels among rival Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders.
Albright's envoys are reduced to negotiating deals on issues which were supposed to be settled under the peace treaty agreed 18 months ago at a U.S. air base in Dayton, Ohio.
Bosnian Moslems now openly discuss the possibility of "the next war" to reverse ethnic expulsions perpretrated by Serb forces during the 1992-95 conflict.
Only the presence of a heavily armed NATO-led force prevents a return to bloodshed.
Although Washington once referred to the Bosnian war as a "European problem", enforcing the U.S.-brokered treaty has become more and more of a headache for the Americans.
In a speech last week, Albright invoked the memory of America's Marshall plan for Western Europe when she urged a renewed commitment to shoring up the peace in Bosnia.
But critics say Washington has refused to take the plunge and fully commit to a leadership role in Bosnia.
By repeatedly threatening to withdraw its peacekeeping troops by mid-1998, critics say the United States has left the impression that it wants to avoid any long-term commitment in Bosnia.

As part of what Washington calls a renewed attempt to fully implement the peace agreement, Albright has pledged more support for independent media and promised to link reconstruction aid to compliance with the Dayton accords .

Albright, who helped establish the U.N. war crimes tribunal, has also led a drive to refocus attention on the extradition of indicted war criminals, most of whom remain at large, continuing to exert influence with impunity.
Tough talk about forcing suspects to face justice has raised expectations that indicted war criminals could be arrested but it remains unclear if Western powers are any closer to taking action.
Albright will first have to make her case to the U.S. military which has so far rejected proposals to launch "manhunts" for prominent suspects such as former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic.

Officers in the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR), who fear "mission creep", are also opposed to suggestions from Albright that NATO may become more involved in helping refugees move back to their homes.

No matter how much energy is devoted to fresh initiatives for Bosnia, political analysts say not much progress can be expected when the country's authoritarian neighbours, Croatia and Serbia, continue to back nationalist proteges in Bosnia.

To avoid another influx of refugees into Western Europe and to counter the influence of Iran and some other Islamic countries, Western diplomats say that NATO will have no choice but to extend its peacekeeping mission beyond 1998.
"We will look over the abyss and realise that staying is easier than withdrawing," said one Western official. "And NATO will reluctantly agree to keeping some sort of force here."
